clue.text: Welsh town archbishop enters further down the hill

indicators.note: the archbishop goes into the phrase for further down the hill, so enters marks a container

parts.note: lower means further down a slope
Cosmo Lang was Archbishop of Canterbury in the 1930s

explanation.surface: A churchman arrives in a Welsh town lying lower down the hillside.
explanation.walkthrough: Cosmo Lang was Archbishop of Canterbury 1928-42; 'enters' slots his surname in after the first letter of the hill phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the name of a small village and community in Gwynedd, North Wales.

clue.text: Baseline match figures produced by him?

definitions.text: Baseline match figures produced by him?

parts.words: Baseline match figures produced by him?
parts.note: reads like tennis statistics, but points to the Salford painter famous for thin matchstick men standing along the bottom of his industrial scenes

explanation.surface: A question about who compiled the scores from a baseline tennis match.
explanation.walkthrough: L. S. Lowry, an English painter, is known for crowds of stick-thin 'matchstick men'; 'Baseline' and 'match' suggest tennis, not painting.
explanation.definitionFit: The painter's crowds are popularly called matchstick figures, drawn standing on the ground line of the canvas.

clue.text: One less retailer, maybe, subject to my changes?

definitions.text: One less retailer, maybe, subject to my changes?

indicators.note: the clue's speaker changes things, so the remaining letters are rearranged
less means the following word loses something, here the letter for one

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A retailer short of one item wonders about being changed by the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: Take I (one) from RETAILER to leave RETALER, then 'subject to my changes' rearranges those letters; the whole clue also describes the speaker, someone who changes things.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who makes changes to things is an alterer, the role the clue's narrator claims.

clue.text: Old song composed enthralling sad trivia bod

definitions.text: Old song composed enthralling sad trivia bod

indicators.note: enthralling means holding captive, so one group of letters encloses the other
composed means put together, so these letters are arranged afresh
sad here means in a sorry state, so the following letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A dreary pub-quiz buff is captivated by an old tune somebody wrote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' rearranges O + SONG into GOONS; 'sad' rearranges TRIVIA BOD into DVIBRATIO; 'enthralling' puts the second inside the first. The whole clue also calls the result an old song: the 1966 Beach Boys hit.
explanation.definitionFit: Good Vibrations is a Beach Boys single from 1966, now a classic old song.

clue.text: Mercifully unlikely to get lost on passing round one

parts.note: a walker carrying a compass is unlikely to lose the way

indicators.note: the last letter is passed round to the front of the short group

parts.note: taken as written
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Someone is told they will not lose their way while circling a landmark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'passing round' moves the I of ONI round to the front, making ION after WITH COMPASS.
explanation.definitionFit: To act mercifully is to act with compassion, showing pity rather than harshness.

clue.text: Map of secluded place for future consideration?

definitions.text: Map of secluded place for future consideration?

parts.words: Map of secluded place for future consideration?
parts.note: a chart of a quiet hideaway, but really the financial arrangement made in working life for the years after work ends

explanation.surface: Someone keeps a chart of a hidden spot to look at later.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a map (plan) of a place of seclusion (retirement), it is also the scheme one makes for life after work.
explanation.definitionFit: A pension or savings scheme arranged for life after stopping work is exactly this kind of forward planning.

clue.text: Find backward soldier getting stuck into afters

indicators.note: backward means the assembled letters are read from right to left
the soldier is put inside the pudding word, so this marks a container

parts.note: afters is British slang for dessert, also called pud
GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A slow-witted soldier tucks into his pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: GI goes into PUD to give PUGID, and 'backward' turns the whole to give DIGUP. 'backward' looks like it describes the soldier as dim.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig something up is to find or unearth it, as with facts or treasure.

clue.text: As exemplified by Spassky offering Fischer a draw?

definitions.text: As exemplified by Spassky offering Fischer a draw?

parts.words: As exemplified by Spassky offering Fischer a draw?
parts.note: a chess turn by the Soviet champion proposing a peaceful end to the game, read as a tactful political gesture

explanation.surface: Recalls the 1972 world chess match between Boris Spassky and Bobby Fischer.
explanation.walkthrough: Spassky (USSR) and Fischer (USA) played the 1972 Cold War world championship; offering a draw is both a chess action and a tactful gesture between superpowers.
explanation.definitionFit: A tactful, peace-seeking step in negotiations is called this, and here it is also a literal chess turn.

clue.text: Forbidding a single sneer

parts.note: a forbidding look is grim
an ace is a single, a one, as on dice or cards

explanation.surface: A stern refusal of even one person, met with contempt.
explanation.definitionFit: A grimace is a twisted facial expression, which can be a sneer of disgust.

clue.text: Dugout location

parts.note: a sheltered pitchside bench in football, but read as dug out, meaning exposed, it points to a tabloid feature with topless models

explanation.surface: A question about where the dugout is at a football ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun newspaper's 'Page Three' long carried photos of topless models; 'dugout' read as 'dug out' (dugs = breasts) is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The tabloid's third page was the place where models appeared with breasts bared.

clue.text: Going on which 12 have no limits

definitions.meaning: going on means continuing without a break
vibrations of a string run its full length when no finger stops the string to shorten it

explanation.walkthrough: 12 is VIBRATIONS. To 'stop' a string is to press it down and shorten its vibrating length, so an open string vibrates without stopping.
explanation.definitionFit: Continuing without stopping means carrying on with no pause; open strings vibrate along their whole length, unshortened.

clue.text: Three 21s back home for Nutkin?

indicators.note: back means the word for the squirrel's home is read in reverse

parts.note: Squirrel Nutkin is a Beatrix Potter squirrel, and a squirrel's nest is a dray (also spelt drey)

explanation.surface: Measuring a squirrel's house in feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 21 is FOOT, so 'Three 21s' is three feet. Squirrel Nutkin is a Beatrix Potter character.
explanation.definitionFit: A yard is an imperial length equal to three feet.

clue.text: Aboard craft, depart with Jason, ultimately seeking gold? I did

definitions.text: Aboard craft, depart with Jason, ultimately seeking gold? I did

indicators.note: aboard means on board, so the following pieces sit inside the word for craft

parts.note: craft means art or skill
depart means go

indicators.note: ultimately points to the last letter of Jason

parts.note: AU is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: A speaker claims to have sailed with Jason in search of the Golden Fleece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aboard' is a container signal: 'on board' the craft word. The whole clue is spoken by one of Jason's crew, who sailed on the Argo for the Golden Fleece.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the crew who sailed with Jason on the Argo to seek the Golden Fleece were called this.

clue.text: See 3
See 4
Section of flyover (M1 for M5) reminiscent of Spaghetti Junction?

annotationWithheld.why: Section of flyover (M1 for M5) reminiscent of Spaghetti Junction? (9): sound hidden word flyoVER M1 FOR M5 where the figure 1 must be read as the letter I; the hidden-word check reads letters only, so the run VERMFORM cannot give VERMIFORM
annotationWithheld.clue: Section of flyover (M1 for M5) reminiscent of Spaghetti Junction?

clue.text: Madam's stand-in at the Palace?

parts.note: a deputy for the monarch at court, but madam also suggests a brothel keeper, a queen of vice

explanation.surface: Wondering who deputises for Her Majesty at Buckingham Palace.
explanation.walkthrough: A madam runs a brothel, a 'vice queen'; a vicequeen is also a woman ruling as the monarch's deputy, as a viceroy would.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman deputising for a queen as ruler is a vicequeen, just as a viceroy deputises for a king.

clue.text: Prince arrived before church deserted

indicators.note: the letters for church abandon the phrase, so they are removed

parts.note: arrived means came
ere is a poetic word for before
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A royal arrived ahead of time to find the church empty.
explanation.walkthrough: CAME + ERE gives CAMEERE; 'deserted' removes C and E (CE, the church) to leave AMEER.
explanation.definitionFit: An ameer, also spelt emir or amir, is a Muslim prince or ruler.

clue.text: Provide for grub, having no support

indicators.note: having no means the word for support is taken away

parts.note: a caterpillar is a larva, a grub
a pillar is a supporting column

explanation.surface: Someone must supply food without any help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grub' looks like food, linking with 'Provide for'; it is a caterpillar.
explanation.definitionFit: To cater is to provide food or what is needed for someone.

clue.text: Major rebellion in the pool, so to speak?

indicators.note: so to speak signals a word said out loud, matched by another spelling

parts.note: what goes on in an office typing pool is typing

explanation.surface: A big uprising in the swimming pool.
explanation.walkthrough: A typing pool was an office of typists. The Taiping Rebellion (1850-64) was a huge civil war in China.
explanation.definitionFit: The Taiping Rebellion in nineteenth-century China was one of the deadliest civil wars in history.

clue.text: Affected thespian has nothing in tights

indicators.note: in means the zero goes inside the rearranged letters
affected means artificially altered, so the word's letters are rearranged

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A pretentious actor wears nothing but tights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affected' rearranges THESPIAN into PANTIHSE, and O (nothing) goes 'in' after the H.
explanation.definitionFit: Pantihose, or pantyhose, are sheer tights worn from waist to toe.

clue.text: Pompous illegal member of 'unt admits corruption

indicators.note: admits means lets in, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: a hunt member is a hound, with the H dropped as in the clue's 'unt; hunting with hounds became illegal in Britain in 2005
rot means decay or corruption

explanation.surface: A self-important member of an outlawed fox hunt confesses to wrongdoing.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped H of 'unt tells you to drop it from HOUND too, giving OUND, which takes in ROT.
explanation.definitionFit: Orotund describes speech or style that is pompous and bombastic.

clue.text: Question Time is shattering a mystical belief

indicators.note: shattering means breaking into pieces, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A TV debate show is wrecking somebody's spiritual faith.
explanation.walkthrough: Question Time is a BBC TV political debate programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Quietism is a Christian mystical doctrine of passive contemplation and surrender to God.

clue.text: Pay for ex-Labour leader

definitions.meaning: to pay a bill is to settle it
Michael, the British Labour Party leader from 1980 to 1983, whose surname is also a body part

explanation.definitionFit: Settling the bill is footing it; Michael Foot was Labour leader in the early 1980s.

clue.text: Drift in continent enormous

indicators.note: in means the answer lies within the following words

explanation.surface: Continental drift is on an enormous scale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drift' suggests continental drift; it means the general gist.
explanation.definitionFit: The tenor of a speech is its general drift or meaning.

clue.text: See 5
See 6
Characters emerging from lair in cloud take me to your leader

indicators.note: letters coming out of the words in new order, so these are rearranged

explanation.surface: An alien steps out of a cloud lair and says the famous line to an earthling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take' joins the second batch of letters; 'leader' is a newspaper's leading article.
explanation.definitionFit: A leader is a newspaper's leading article, the editorial setting out the paper's own view.

clue.text: "Hot drink", perhaps, back of tabloid covers

indicators.note: covers means one piece wraps round the other
back of means the tabloid's name is read in reverse

parts.note: the Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
eg, for example, signals perhaps

explanation.surface: A hot drink is advertised on the back of a tabloid newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back of' reverses SUN to NUS, which 'covers' EG. The quotes hint that 'Hot drink' may be just one sense: Negus is also an Ethiopian king's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Negus is a hot drink of port or sherry with sugar, lemon and spice.

clue.text: Running errand with one terribly illiterate

indicators.note: terribly means badly, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Somebody makes a hash of an errand with somebody who cannot read.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running' only sets the scene of an errand; 'terribly' is the signal to rearrange ERRAND + ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A non-reader cannot read, so an illiterate person, used as a noun, fits the swap.
